897.title: Mourning as devotion
897.hook: in Muharram many Shia communities hold majalis, recite elegies and serve water
897.howItsDone: In Muharram, Shia communities hold majalis, gatherings where a speaker retells Karbala and reciters chant elegies, and some set out water and food for passersby in Husayn's memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghaybah, the Twelver Shia belief that the twelfth Imam is hidden and will return. Your line was awaiting justice.

A hall with the lights turned low. Black cloth on the walls. People sit on the floor, shoulder to shoulder, and someone at the front begins to speak about a camp by a river. Halfway through, a voice rises into a chant, and the room answers. Some beat their chests in rhythm. Some cover their faces. By the door, a table with jugs of water and cups for anyone walking past. This is a majlis in Muharram, and in Shia communities it can happen night after night. To an outsider it can look like grief that will not end. Shia teachers call it something closer to love. Today: mourning as devotion.

A majlis is simply a sitting, a gathering. In Muharram it becomes a gathering to remember Husayn. A speaker retells Karbala, often one person or one moment each night: the thirst, al-Abbas at the river, Zaynab's voice. Then come the elegies, poems of grief sung or chanted, and the room weeps. Why weep for someone who died so long ago? Shia teachers answer: because we love him, and because the Prophet ﷺ loved him. Tears for Husayn are tears for the Prophet's own grandson, a way of standing with the Prophet's family. The weeping is the point, not a side effect. Tears themselves have a place in Islam. When the Prophet's infant son Ibrahim was dying, the hadith says, the Prophet's eyes filled with tears. Someone was surprised. He said, in effect: the eye weeps and the heart grieves, but we say only what pleases our Lord. Grief is not a failure of faith. The Qur'an gives the words believers say when loss arrives: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Mourning held like this faces God rather than turning away. Then the water. Because the camp at Karbala was kept from the river, Shia communities in Muharram set out water for strangers. A cup handed to someone you'll never see again becomes a small act of remembrance. Grief that ends in service. Grief as love.

Bring to mind someone you have lost, or someone you love who is far away, and let the grief be there without hurrying it off. Notice whose face comes with it. If you pray, ask God's mercy for that person in your own words; if you don't, simply stay with them for a few breaths.
Majlis, a sitting, a gathering: in Muharram, the gathering where Shia Muslims retell Karbala, weep for Husayn, and set out water, offering grief itself as love. Today's word.
Your line: grief as love. Tears can be a way of staying close. See you tomorrow.

898.title: The four in Sunni reckoning
898.hook: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali: the Rightly Guided Caliphs for Sunni Muslims
898.howItsDone: Sunni Muslims name Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali together as the Rightly Guided Caliphs, often adding 'may God be pleased with him' after each name, and some Friday sermons mention all four.

segments.voice: Yesterday: majlis, the Muharram gathering, and the water at the door. Your line was grief as love.

Four names, in order. Abu Bakr. Umar. Uthman. Ali. Each has had his own days on this path: a first speech, a register, a single reading of the Qur'an, a shield brought before a judge. In Sunni Islam, those four names are also said together, in that order, as one group with one title. In a Friday sermon, the preacher may name all four and ask God to be pleased with them. Today: the four in Sunni reckoning.

The title is al-khulafa' al-rashidun: the rightly guided caliphs. Khulafa' is the plural of khalifah, successor, the one who comes after. Rashidun means rightly guided, people who walk on the straight road. The phrase leans on a hadith. In it, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gives his companions a farewell counsel: hold to my way, and the way of the rightly guided successors after me, and grip it tightly. Sunni scholars read those successors as these four. Each of the four came to office by a different route. The Sunni telling looks at those four doors and sees one community walking through all of them, so the four belong together, in that order. Their time is held up as the model of what rule under God should look like, even with its wars and its grief. Here is the detail worth keeping. Ali stands fourth in this Sunni list. In Shia Islam, Ali stands first, as the first Imam. The same man, honored in both, counted from a different place. Sunni Muslims love Ali as the fourth of the four and as the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law. Shia Muslims love him as the one the Prophet named. Neither side leaves him out. Today, the four.

Say the four names quietly, in order, one per breath: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali, and with each, recall one thing from his days on this path: a speech, a register, a page, a shield. In Sunni practice each name is followed by: may God be pleased with him. If you pray, you can add it too.
Al-khulafa' al-rashidun. The rightly guided caliphs: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, named together, in order, in Sunni Islam. Today's word.
Your line: the four. Fourth here, first there, and loved in both. Day eight hundred ninety-eight, done.

899.title: The family, loved by all
899.hook: every prayer asks blessings on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad
899.howItsDone: In the sitting of the daily prayer, Sunni and Shia Muslims ask blessings on Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and the short salawat is also said when the Prophet's name is mentioned.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rightly guided caliphs, Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali. Your line was the four.

The companions had a question. They already knew how to greet the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: peace be upon you. But the Qur'an had told them something more, to ask blessings on him. So how, exactly? What words? The hadith says he answered them with a short prayer, and it did not stop at his own name. It reached past him, to his family. Today: the family, loved by all.
screen: `HOW DO WE ASK BLESSINGS ON YOU?`

segments.voice: The verse behind the question says: "Lo! Allah and His angels shower blessings on the Prophet. O ye who believe! Ask blessings on him and salute him with a worthy salutation." When the companions asked how, the hadith in al-Bukhari gives his reply. Its opening words: O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham. Notice two things. The family is in the prayer by the Prophet's own choice: he was asked about himself, and he added them. And he set it beside Abraham and his household, a family the Qur'an itself honors. The Arabic phrase is al Muhammad, the family of Muhammad. Scholars discuss who it includes. In Shia teaching it points above all to Ali, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, and the Imams after them. Sunni scholars have read it as his household, some more widely. But the love is shared. Words from this prayer are said in the sitting of the daily prayer, in Sunni and Shia practice alike. A poem attributed to the Sunni jurist al-Shafi'i says, in effect: O family of God's Messenger, love of you is a duty God revealed. After weeks of a hard story, here Sunni and Shia Muslims say the same names in the same breath. On him and his family.
screen: then, large: `ON HIM AND HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the short blessing known as the salawat slowly, once per breath: Allahumma salli ala Muhammad wa ala ali Muhammad, O God, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad. On the word family, bring to mind the names: Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, Husayn. If you don't pray, simply hold those names, one per breath, and let them be people rather than titles.
The family. Al Muhammad, the household of the Prophet, whom he named in the blessing he taught, and whom Sunni and Shia Muslims both love. Today's word.
Your line: on him and his family. He was asked about himself, and he named them too. That's day eight hundred ninety-nine.

900.title: What is shared
900.hook: one Allah, one Prophet ﷺ, one Qur'an, one qiblah, five prayers
900.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims share the Qur'an, the five daily prayers facing the Kaaba, the Ramadan fast and the pilgrimage to Mecca; differences such as hand position or combining prayer times sit within that shared practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the family, blessed in the prayer by Sunni and Shia alike. Your line was on him and his family.

Try a short list. One God. One Prophet, Muhammad ﷺ. One Qur'an, the same words in the same order. One direction to face, the Kaaba in Mecca. Prayer, day and night, bowing and putting the forehead to the ground. The fast of Ramadan. The pilgrimage to the same house, walking around it in the same direction. That list is true for a Sunni Muslim in one city and a Shia Muslim in another. After a long look at a split, here is the other column. Today: what is shared.

A hadith in al-Bukhari draws the line with almost nothing. The Prophet said, in effect: whoever prays our prayer, faces our qiblah, and eats what we slaughter, that one is a Muslim, under the protection of God and His Messenger. Three plain, outward things: a prayer, a direction, a meal. That is the whole measure this report gives. Then the Qur'an: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A rope, held by many hands. The verse doesn't ask everyone to stand in the same spot on the rope. It asks them to keep holding it. Now the qiblah, the direction you face. Muslims in prayer turn toward the same house, so the rows of the whole world, seen from above, would form rings around one center. Sunni and Shia alike. Even the differences sit inside the shared. Both pray the five daily prayers; Shia practice allows gathering them into three times of day, and Sunni schools allow joining them in certain cases, such as travel. Tomorrow looks at the smaller differences you can see in a row of worshipers; they too sit inside one prayer, facing one way. The split was real, and the grief was real. But set the two lists side by side, and see which one runs longer. More shared than split.

If you are Muslim, count on your fingers, one item per breath, what you share with every Muslim: God, the Prophet, the Qur'an, the qiblah, the prayer, the fast, the pilgrimage. If you're not, make the same kind of list with someone you differ from, what you both love, fear and hope for, and let it grow longer than you expected.
Qiblah, the direction faced in prayer: toward the Kaaba, the same for Sunni and Shia Muslims, alongside one God, one Prophet, one Qur'an, and one prayer. Today's word.
Your line: more shared than split. Every row on earth bends around one center. Nine hundred days now.

901.title: Sunni and Shia today
901.hook: Sunni and Shia Muslims today, two families of one faith, praying side by side
901.tomorrow: Block C close: the wound and the healing
901.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims perform the same pilgrimage rites in Mecca, and in some cities pray in the same mosques; Shia worshipers prostrate on earth, such as a clay tablet, and pray with arms at their sides, as some Maliki Sunnis also do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: qiblah, one direction for every row. Your line was more shared than split.

A row of people in prayer, shoulder to shoulder. The man on the left has his hands folded over his chest. The man on the right lets his arms hang at his sides. When they go down into prostration, one sets his forehead on a small disc of baked clay he carried in his pocket. The other puts his forehead straight on the carpet. Then they rise at the same moment, facing the same way. From the back of the room you might guess one is Sunni and one is Shia. You might be wrong. Today: Sunni and Shia today.

Sunni and Shia Muslims share cities, streets, and sometimes houses. At the pilgrimage in Mecca, pilgrims from both walk around the same Kaaba, stand on the same plain of Arafat, and throw stones at the same pillars. No one checks which telling of the succession you hold. In some cities there are mosques where both pray in the same rows. In some families, a Sunni mother and a Shia father, or the reverse, raise children who know both ways of standing. The differences you can see are small and real. Shia practice is to pray with arms at the sides and to prostrate on natural earth, such as a clay tablet called a turbah, since Shia jurists teach that the forehead should rest on earth or what grows from it. Folded hands are the Sunni posture people tend to picture. But in the Maliki school of Sunni law, praying with arms at the sides is an accepted practice too. So the hands alone sort nobody. And scholars of the schools, Sunni and Shia, have put their names to a statement issued in Amman, recognizing one another's schools as Muslim and saying their followers may not be declared outside the faith. Statements don't end every quarrel. But they say where the scholars chose to stand. Side by side.

Picture a line of people in prayer, each standing a little differently, all facing one way, and put yourself in the line. Then bring to mind someone you live or work beside who sees the world differently from you, and stand with them there, in your mind, for a few breaths.

Turbah, earth or soil: the clay tablet some Shia worshipers rest their foreheads on in prostration, one of the small, visible differences between Sunni and Shia Muslims who pray in the same rows. Today's word.
Your line: side by side. Different hands, the same row, the same moment. Day nine hundred one.

902.title: Block C close: the wound and the healing
902.hook: a split remembered with grief, and a family everyone loves
902.howItsDone: Sunni and Shia Muslims remember the early conflicts in different ways, in sermons, histories and Muharram gatherings, and the Qur'an's prayer for 'our brethren who were before us in the faith' (59:10) is recited as a prayer against rancor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: turbah, hands folded and hands at the sides, one row. Your line was side by side.

It began on the day after. The Prophet ﷺ had died, his body was not yet buried, and the community had to decide who would lead. Then came a pledge in a meeting hall. A pool called Ghadir Khumm. A calendar, a Coptic boy's case, a plague. A caliph killed at home, a battle around a camel, a field called Siffin. Hasan's peace, Husayn's refusal, a river cut off, Zaynab's voice. It's a hard stretch of history, and it has been told two ways. Today the block closes. Today: the wound and the healing.
screen: `A POOL, A CALENDAR, A FIELD, A RIVER.`

segments.voice: Start with the wound. The question of who should lead after the Prophet was answered one way by those who pledged to Abu Bakr, and another way by those who held that the Prophet had named Ali. Out of those answers came the Sunni telling and the Shia telling, and both carried their grief: Uthman killed while reading the Qur'an, Ali struck in the mosque at Kufa, Husayn at Karbala. Neither tradition hides the wound. It is remembered, in sermons and in majalis. Now the healing, which was there all along. The same family is loved on both sides; the blessing on Muhammad and his family is said in prayer by both. The four caliphs and the twelve Imams have one man in common, Ali. The qiblah doesn't move for anyone. And the Qur'an gives words for people who come after an earlier generation. After praising the emigrants and the helpers of Medina, it describes believers who came later and say: "Our Lord! Forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancour toward those who believe." That prayer doesn't settle who was right. It asks forgiveness for everyone before us, and a heart without rancor toward everyone now. Read this way, unity isn't an agreement reached. It's something asked for, again and again. Unity is a prayer. Next, the path leaves the split behind and walks into the cities the Muslims built.

If you pray, say the Qur'an's words slowly: Our Lord, forgive us and our brethren who were before us in the faith, and place not in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe. If you don't, bring to mind one rift you know, in a family, a friendship or a community, and hold both sides of it without choosing, breathing in for those who came before and out for those here now.
Ghill, rancor, a grudge in the heart: the word the Qur'an's prayer asks God to remove, closing this block on the wound of the first split and the healing held in common. Today's word.
Your line: unity is a prayer. It doesn't wait for anyone to win the argument. That's a block closed.

903.title: A capital in Damascus
903.hook: the Umayyads rule from Damascus over lands from Spain to Sindh
903.howItsDone: Muslim histories tell the Umayyad period, ruled from Damascus, as a time of wide expansion, and Sunni and Shia teachers judge its rulers differently.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ghill, the grudge the Qur'an's prayer asks God to remove. Your line was unity is a prayer.

Put one finger on the Atlantic coast of Spain, where the land runs out into ocean. Put another on the Indus River, in Sindh, in what is now Pakistan. Between your fingers: North Africa, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Persia. Under the Umayyad caliphs, one ruling house in Damascus claimed all of it: Arabs, Berbers, Copts, Greeks, Persians and many more, under one government. A new block begins: Islamic history and civilization. Today: a capital in Damascus.

The Umayyads are a clan of Quraysh, the Prophet's own tribe, and their line of caliphs began with Mu'awiyah, already met on this path, ruling from Damascus. Today the path looks at what that seat became. Damascus was an old city long before Islam, a crossroads of caravans. From there, Umayyad armies and governors pushed west across North Africa and into Spain, which Muslims called al-Andalus, and east into Central Asia and Sindh. That's the plain history: an empire, built partly by conquest, with all the costs conquest carries. The people of these lands did not all become Muslim at once. Churches and synagogues went on, and the histories suggest the change of faith came slowly, family by family. A capital ruling so many peoples has a practical problem: how do you run it? At first, by keeping the old offices. Clerks in Syria went on keeping records in Greek, as they had under Byzantium. Clerks in Iraq and Persia kept them in Persian. The Qur'an had already spoken to a world of many peoples: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." A capital in Damascus held them under one roof, and from that mix came mosques, coins, books and cities. From Spain to Sindh.
screen: `NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: If you have a map nearby, find Spain and the Indus River and let your eyes travel slowly between them, naming each region as you pass: Morocco, Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Iran. Then close your eyes and bring to mind the people of those places, then and now: farmers, clerks, merchants, families at prayer in mosques, churches and synagogues.
Damascus. The old crossroads city that became the Umayyad capital, from which armies and governors reached from al-Andalus to Sindh. Today's word.
Your line: from spain to sindh. Nations and tribes, that they may know one another. Until tomorrow.

options: At first by keeping old offices: Greek records in Syria, Persian in Iraq.
By making everyone convert and switch to Arabic right away.
